# the ten most frequent missing value patterns
# TRUE means missing


# Is the pattern monotone?
#
# If the variables are ordered so that the number of missing values only
# increases from left to right, and if a respondent missing on one variable
# is also missing on every later variable, the pattern is monotone. This is
# typical for a questionnaire that respondents abandon partway through: they
# answer up to a point and then stop.
#
# Compare the column sums above with the patterns table. If the frequent
# patterns are all of the form "observed ... observed, missing ... missing",
# the pattern is monotone. Isolated gaps in the middle mean it is not.

Select the complete observations and compute the mean.

hin95_complete <- hin95 |>
  filter(nvalid == n_items) |>
  mutate(
    rs_mean = rowMeans(pick(rs272:rs286))
  )
# no na.rm is needed here because these rows have no missing values


hin95_complete |>
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    mean_of_means = mean(rs_mean)
  )

     n mean_of_means
1 1694      3.071271

# the mean of the mean-variable over the complete cases

Compute the mean over the available values, for all respondents.

hin95 <- hin95 |>
  mutate(
    rs_mean_available = if_else(
      nvalid == 0,
      NA_real_,
      rowMeans(pick(rs272:rs286), na.rm = TRUE)
    )
  )
# rowMeans(na.rm = TRUE) returns NaN, not NA, for a row with no valid values
# the if_else() turns those rows into a proper missing value


hin95 |>
  summarise(
    n_valid_scale = sum(!is.na(rs_mean_available)),
    mean_available = mean(rs_mean_available, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

  n_valid_scale mean_available
1          3082        2.98348

# compare with the complete-case mean above
# a difference between the two suggests that respondents with missing values
# differ systematically from respondents without them



4. Education of the same-sex parent

# The construction itself is one line, but the missing values need thought.
# There are three sources of missingness, and they are not equivalent.
#
# 1. male is missing. We do not know which parent to look at, so ssedu must
#    be missing, even if both feduc and meduc are observed.
# 2. The same-sex parent's education is missing. Then ssedu is missing:
#    that is precisely the value we wanted.
# 3. The OTHER parent's education is missing. This is irrelevant. A woman
#    with an observed meduc should get a value for ssedu even if feduc is
#    missing. Code that is careless about this throws away usable cases.
#
# if_else() handles all three correctly: it propagates NA from the condition,
# and it evaluates only the branch that applies.


data <- data |>
  mutate(
    ssedu = if_else(male == 1, feduc, meduc)
  )
# male == 1 gives NA when male is missing, so ssedu becomes NA
# for men the father's education is taken, for women the mother's

title: Using functions
text: In this part you will learn about the use of functions (such as “take the square root”, ‘”taking a substring of a string”, or “draw a random number” —the computer version of “flipping coins”— to accomplish various tasks in constructing or modifying variables. Functions may be embedded in arithmetic expressions, and they may also be composed. For instance, we may take the logarithm of a random variate with a uniform distribution on [0, 1]. We present the information, mostly in the context of assignments, under a number of headers:

title: Using functions
text:
Examples
Absolute difference dage of the age of husband (hage) and wife (wage):

data <- data |>   
  mutate(dage = abs(wage - hage)) 

Equivalent, using if_else():

data <- data |>   
  mutate(dage = if_else(wage > hage, wage - hage, hage - wage)) 

The natural logarithm of 1 + wagerate. Note that log(x) is missing for x <= 0.

data <- data |>   
  mutate(lnwage = log(1 + wagerate)) 

The maximum wage rate of the husband (hwage) and wife (wwage):

data <- data |>   
  mutate(maxwage = pmax(hwage, wwage)) 

Income chopped at 100000:

data <- data |>   
  mutate(rinc = pmin(inc, 100000)) 

Length, number of characters, in the string variable cityname:

data <- data |>   
  mutate(nch = nchar(cityname)) 

Display the number of full weeks in a year. The R Console can be used as an interactive calculator.

floor(365 / 7) 

Embellish unrounded output.

paste("number of full weeks in year =", round(365 / 7, 2)) 


Numeric functions

The following functions in R are important for the creation of new variables or the modification of existing variables. Make sure that you understand the functions. If you are uncertain, think of examples, and verify. In particular, check how to access the help pages for their definitions. Be sure to understand that these functions exist, roughly what they are good for, and how to find the details at the moment you really want to use them.




R
Description




sqrt(x)
square-root of x


abs(x)
the absolute value of x


pmin(x, y)
the minimum of x and y


pmax(x, y, z)
the maximum of x, y, and z


round(x)
x rounded to nearest integer


floor(x)
x rounded down


ceiling(x)
x rounded up


x %% y
remainder after dividing x by y


exp(x)
the exponential function


log(x)
the natural logarithm


log10(x)
the logarithm to the base 10



Functions and ordinary expressions may be mixed. For instance, you may write:
data <- data |>   
  mutate(lp = (log(p) / log(1 - p)) - 4) 
Functions may also be nested, or composed. For instance:
data <- data |>   
  mutate(fx = log(1 + exp(x))) 
Use parentheses if you are unsure about the priority of operators. What comes first, division or subtraction? Many inexperienced users will not remember, it is division. We recommend using parentheses rather than relying on your memory.
For each of these functions, what do you think will happen if the argument, or any of the arguments, is missing? Under what other conditions can each of these functions return a missing value? Experiment, or read the help pages.

Check the meaning of the following mathematical R functions.








R
Description




x %in% c(a, b, c, ...)
logical: x equals a, b, c, …


between(x, a, b)
logical: x ≥ a and x ≤ b


if_else(x, y, z)
if x, then y else z


case_when()
recode values using multiple conditions


cut(x, breaks)
recode a continuous variable into intervals


pmin(pmax(x, a), b)
x if a ≤ x ≤ b, b if x > b, a if x < a





String functions
In R, string manipulation is commonly performed using functions from the stringr package, which is part of the tidyverse. Make sure that you understand the purpose of the following functions. If you are uncertain, think of examples and verify them.



R
Description




str_length(s)
length of string


str_to_lower(s)
convert string s to lowercase


str_to_upper(s)
convert string s to uppercase


str_detect(s, t)
test whether string t occurs in string s


str_locate(s, t)
position of string t in string s


str_sub(s, n, m)
substring of s from position n to m


str_trim(s)
drops leading and trailing blanks from s


as.numeric(s)
convert string s to a number


as.character(x)
convert object x to a string



You may compute the length of a string variable str as:
data <- data |>   
  mutate(len = str_length(str)) 
To turn a string variable into lowercase:
data <- data |>   
  mutate(ustr = str_to_lower(str)) 
As a more demanding task, split a string variable str into the first word (w1) and the remainder of the string (rest), where the first word is defined as all characters up to the first space.
data <- data |>   
  mutate(     
    fspace = str_locate(str, " ")[, 1],     
    w1 = if_else(       
    !is.na(fspace),       
    str_sub(str, 1, fspace - 1),       
    str     
  ),     
  rest = if_else(       
    !is.na(fspace),       
    str_sub(str, fspace + 1),       
    ""     
    )   
  ) 
Does this code yield correct results if str has one or more leading spaces? Can you fix it? Can you think of a way to extract the second word?
The functions as.numeric() and as.character() convert between strings and numeric values. When as.numeric() cannot interpret a string as a number, it returns NA.
In the assignments below you will apply string functions to manipulate dates and name-address information.


Other functions in R
There are plenty of other types of R functions. We do not expect you to remember all details of these or any of the other functions you encounter here, just that you get an understanding of the kinds of tasks that may be accomplished with functions, and how to access information about them when needed.
(a) Random number generation

runif(1) draws a random number from the uniform distribution on the interval [0,1). Each time you invoke runif(), the function returns a different value. sample(1:5, 1) returns 1, 2, …, 5 each with the same probability.
rbinom(1, 1, 0.75) generates a 1 with probability 0.75, and a 0 with probability 0.25.
rbinom(1, 1, 0.5) generates 0 and 1 with equal probability.
rnorm(1, 1.3, 2.5) generates a random number from a normal distribution with mean = 1.3 and standard deviation = 2.5.

For instance, to randomly select each observation in the data with probability 0.5:
data <- data |>   
  mutate(filter = rbinom(n(), 1, 0.5))  

data |>   filter(filter == 1) |>   
  summarise(mean_inc = mean(inc, na.rm = TRUE)) 
See ?Distributions for additional random number generators.
(b) Missing value handling
The function is.na() returns TRUE if a value is missing and FALSE otherwise.
For instance, to select all observations that are not missing on the variables age, medu, and gender:
data <- data |>   
  mutate(     
  hasmiss = is.na(age) |       
  is.na(medu) |       
  is.na(gender)   )  
  
  data |>   filter(!hasmiss) 
or equivalently
data <- data |>   
  mutate(     
  notmiss =       
  !is.na(age) &       
  !is.na(medu) &       
  !is.na(gender)   )  
  
  data |>   
    filter(notmiss) 
(c) Miscellaneous

row_number() returns the observation sequence number, that is, 1 in the first observation, 2 in the second observation, etc. One common application is to generate a case identifier:

data <- data |>   
  mutate(respnr = row_number()) 

n() returns the number of observations. Within .by or group_by(), it returns the number of observations in the group.

To list some variables for the oldest person in a household, indexed by hrespnr:
data |>   
  filter(age == max(age), .by = hrespnr) |>   
  select(age, edu, smoking)

title: Using functions
text:
Assignments

Use sbs399.dta. We focus on the variable hrinc (hourly income).


What is the value of the mean and median of the untransformed variable?
For each of the following transformations, find the mean and the median: exp(hrinc), hrinc*hrinc, sqrt(hrinc), log(hrinc), hrinc (i.e., untransformed, identity), 1/sqrt(hrinc), 1/hrinc, and 1/(hrinc*hrinc).
For which transformation, including the no-transformation, is the variable most symmetrically distributed? You may gauge the symmetry of a distribution by its skewness. Recall: a positive skewness indicates a distribution tilted to the left, a negative skewness indicates a distribution tilted to the right. Compare using the function skewness() from the package moments.
Create histograms and density plots of these and some additional transformations of the variable. Apply your code to the first 50 cases only.


The dataset sbs399 contains the variable hrinc, the hourly wage rate. The values are decimal numbers such as 3.5. Generate transformations of this variable using functions:


round hrinc to the nearest integer (so any value between 3.5 and 4.5 should be rounded to 4);
round the variable down (so any value between 3 and 4 is rounded to 3);
round the variable up (so any value between 3 and 4 is rounded to 4);
round in multiples of 10 (so any value between 5 and 15 is rounded to 10);
clip to the range [10,50], i.e., values below 10 are set to 10; values above 50 are set to 50; values between 10 and 50 are returned unchanged.


The dataset sbs399 contains the educational level of the father and mother of respondents (feduc and meduc respectively). We define the educational resources of the parents (peduc) as the maximum of the educational levels of the parents.

Give code to create peduc.
Do you think that this conceptualization is also appropriate if education is seen as a proxy for attitudes?

You want to compute the geographic distance d(h,w) between a subject’s home address and a subject’s work address. Your data contain the geographic coordinates (home_x, home_y) and (work_x, work_y) of the home and work location, expressed as east-west and north-south distances from a reference point in the Netherlands, in units of 1 km, rounded. Give R code that computes the distance d between home and work, assuming a flat earth. Recall that by Pythagoras’ theorem

\[d(h,w) = \sqrt{(home_x - work_x)^2 + (home_y - work_y)^2}\]
Did you dream of ever using this in the social sciences? Round the distance in meaningful units, as locations are rounded in 1 km units, it does not make sense that distance is expressed in a finer unit, say meters. Perform these computations for the home_work dataset that includes 3 cases only.
For the interested reader: How do you obtain such location information yourself? If the dataset contains address information or postal codes, it is possible to use geocoding tools to obtain geolocations. Such tools can add new variables with cleaned address information and geographic coordinates.
Using these geolocations you may compute, as explained above, the distance as the crow flies assuming a flat earth. If you pedantically want to account for the curvature of the earth, R also has packages that compute distances using geographic coordinates on the surface of the earth. More advanced students can even take into account that due to its spinning, the earth has to a high degree of accuracy an ellipsoid shape, not a ball shape. Then again, for a small country as the Netherlands such fine points are fully immaterial.
Additional tools and packages provide access to other map services, such as the travel distance and travel time between two locations, distinguishing travel by car, by public transportation, by bike, and walking. One can also add variables with facilities, e.g., the number of schools within a 2 km radius around a location.

Use the dataset hin95_birthdates.


This dataset contains the respondent’s birth date rbirth, a numeric variable recording the birth dates in the format ddmmyy. Note that the number has 5 digits if dd < 10, and 6 digits otherwise. Construct three variables d_rbirth, m_rbirth, and y_rbirth with the day, month, and year in which the respondent was born. Use the functions %% and floor().
List the first twenty observations to verify your variable construction.
To check your work, you may actually reconstruct the original coding from the three variables, and verify that the reconstructed variable matches the original variable.


The file hin95_birthdates contains the respondent’s birth date as a string variable rbirth_str in the format "ddmmyy". The string is of length 5 if dd < 10, and of length 6 otherwise. Use string functions, to construct three variables with the day, month, and year in which the respondent was born.
The dataset hin95_naw contains name, address, and city information. This is a random selection of address information that we purchased from the Dutch mail agency for the “Households in the Netherlands in 1995” project. In this assignment we do some manipulations of this dataset with address information.


The string variable postcode contains postcodes, compare zip codes, in the Dutch format 1234 AB. Construct a new numeric variable npcode that contains the numeric part. Thus, from 1234 AB we want to extract the part 1234. This is useful to merge information that is being organized with respect to geographic information, e.g., for contextual analyses. First take the substring of the first initial characters, i.e., convert 1234 AB to a string 1234. Then convert this string to a number, thus the string 1234 to the number 1234. Be sure to understand the difference. What is the mean value of npcode? How do you interpret this number?
The string variable plaats contains the alphabetic string for the city in which people live. In R, string variables can often be used directly, but for modelling and categorical summaries it is often useful to convert such a string variable into a factor. Convert plaats into a factor. The numeric codes themselves are not important, this is a nominal variable. Obviously, you do not want to do this by hand for all approximately 600 cities. Read the help page for factor() to find out more about this conversion.

title: Using functions
text:
Answers
Make sure this file is in the same R Project as the data folder. Use relative file paths, not full paths to your computer.

library(tidyverse)

✔ dplyr     1.2.1     ✔ readr     2.2.0

✔ purrr     1.2.2

✖ dplyr::filter() masks stats::filter()
✖ dplyr::lag()    masks stats::lag()
ℹ Use the conflicted package (<http://conflicted.r-lib.org/>) to force all conflicts to become errors

library(haven)
library(moments)

sbs399 <- read_dta("data/sbs399.dta")


1. Transformations of hourly income
The mean and the median of the untransformed variable.

sbs399 |>
  summarise(
    mean_hrinc = mean(hrinc, na.rm = TRUE),
    median_hrinc = median(hrinc, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

# A tibble: 1 × 2
  mean_hrinc median_hrinc
       <dbl>        <dbl>
1       18.2         16.1

# mean and median of hrinc

Before transforming, check the range of hrinc. Several of the transformations below are undefined for values of zero or less.

summary(sbs399$hrinc)

   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max.     NAs 
   0.10   13.40   16.10   18.16   20.20  100.00    1381 

# log() and 1/x are problematic if hrinc can be 0 or negative
# exp() overflows to Inf for large values of hrinc

Create all eight transformations in one step.

transformed <- sbs399 |>
  transmute(
    identity = hrinc,
    exponential = exp(hrinc),
    square = hrinc * hrinc,
    square_root = sqrt(hrinc),
    logarithm = log(hrinc),
    inverse_root = 1 / sqrt(hrinc),
    inverse = 1 / hrinc,
    inverse_square = 1 / (hrinc * hrinc)
  )
# transmute() keeps only the newly created variables

Compute the mean, median, and skewness for each transformation.

transformed |>
  pivot_longer(
    everything(),
    names_to = "transformation",
    values_to = "value"
  ) |>
  summarise(
    n_finite = sum(is.finite(value)),
    mean = mean(value[is.finite(value)]),
    median = median(value[is.finite(value)]),
    skewness = skewness(value[is.finite(value)]),
    .by = transformation
  ) |>
  arrange(abs(skewness))

# A tibble: 8 × 5
  transformation n_finite     mean        median skewness
  <chr>             <int>    <dbl>         <dbl>    <dbl>
1 square_root        1969 4.17e+ 0       4.01        2.04
2 logarithm          1969 2.81e+ 0       2.78       -2.34
3 identity           1969 1.82e+ 1      16.1         4.42
4 square             1969 4.19e+ 2     259.          9.05
5 exponential        1969 1.09e+41 9820675.         15.6 
6 inverse_root       1969 2.54e- 1       0.249      18.9 
7 inverse            1969 8.05e- 2       0.0621     25.0 
8 inverse_square     1969 1.59e- 1       0.00386    25.6 

# transformations are sorted by absolute skewness, so the most symmetric comes first
# is.finite() removes both NA and the Inf values produced by exp() and 1/x

The transformation with the skewness closest to zero is the most symmetric one. Note how strongly exp() and 1/(hrinc*hrinc) distort the distribution: a single large value dominates the mean, while the median barely moves.
Histograms of the transformations, for the first 50 cases only.

transformed |>
  slice(1:50) |>
  pivot_longer(
    everything(),
    names_to = "transformation",
    values_to = "value"
  ) |>
  filter(is.finite(value)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = value)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 15) +
  facet_wrap(~transformation, scales = "free") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Count")







# scales = "free" is needed because the transformations live on very different scales

Density plots of the same transformations.

transformed |>
  slice(1:50) |>
  pivot_longer(
    everything(),
    names_to = "transformation",
    values_to = "value"
  ) |>
  filter(is.finite(value)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = value)) +
  geom_density() +
  facet_wrap(~transformation, scales = "free") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Density")







# a density plot smooths the histogram, which is helpful with only 50 cases



2. Rounding the hourly wage rate

sbs399 <- sbs399 |>
  mutate(
    hrinc_round = round(hrinc),
    hrinc_down = floor(hrinc),
    hrinc_up = ceiling(hrinc),
    hrinc_tens = round(hrinc / 10) * 10,
    hrinc_clip = pmin(pmax(hrinc, 10), 50)
  )
# round()   rounds to the nearest integer
# floor()   always rounds down
# ceiling() always rounds up
# dividing by 10, rounding, and multiplying by 10 gives multiples of 10
# pmin(pmax(x, 10), 50) clips the values to the interval [10, 50]

Inspect the result for the first ten cases.

sbs399 |>
  select(hrinc, hrinc_round, hrinc_down, hrinc_up, hrinc_tens, hrinc_clip) |>
  slice(1:10)

# A tibble: 10 × 6
   hrinc hrinc_round hrinc_down hrinc_up hrinc_tens hrinc_clip
   <dbl>       <dbl>      <dbl>    <dbl>      <dbl>      <dbl>

 5  NA            NA         NA       NA         NA       NA

 9  21.1          21         21       22         20       21.1
10  NA            NA         NA       NA         NA       NA  

# compare the transformations side by side

Check the range of the clipped variable.

range(sbs399$hrinc_clip, na.rm = TRUE)

[1] 10 50

# the minimum should be 10 and the maximum 50

A warning about round(): R rounds halves to the nearest even number, so round(2.5) is 2 and round(3.5) is 4.

round(c(0.5, 1.5, 2.5, 3.5, 4.5))

[1] 0 2 2 4 4

# this is the IEEE standard, not a bug



3. Educational resources of the parents

sbs399 <- sbs399 |>
  mutate(
    peduc = pmax(feduc, meduc)
  )
# pmax() compares the two variables element by element, respondent by respondent
# max(feduc, meduc) would return one single number for the whole dataset

Check the new variable.

sbs399 |>
  select(feduc, meduc, peduc) |>
  slice(1:10)

# A tibble: 10 × 3
   feduc                   meduc                   peduc                  
   <dbl+lbl>               <dbl+lbl>               <dbl+lbl>              
 1 1 [elementary [lo]]     2 [lower vocat [lbo]]   2 [lower vocat [lbo]]  
 2 3 [lower second [mavo]] 1 [elementary [lo]]     3 [lower second [mavo]]
 3 1 [elementary [lo]]     2 [lower vocat [lbo]]   2 [lower vocat [lbo]]  
 4 1 [elementary [lo]]     1 [elementary [lo]]     1 [elementary [lo]]    
 5 2 [lower vocat [lbo]]   2 [lower vocat [lbo]]   2 [lower vocat [lbo]]  
 6 1 [elementary [lo]]     1 [elementary [lo]]     1 [elementary [lo]]    
 7 5 [higher second [vwo]] 2 [lower vocat [lbo]]   5 [higher second [vwo]]
 8 1 [elementary [lo]]     1 [elementary [lo]]     1 [elementary [lo]]    
 9 1 [elementary [lo]]     1 [elementary [lo]]     1 [elementary [lo]]    
10 2 [lower vocat [lbo]]   3 [lower second [mavo]] 3 [lower second [mavo]]

# peduc should equal the larger of the two parental education levels


# Is the maximum appropriate if education proxies attitudes?
#
# For resources the maximum is defensible: the better educated parent can
# supply help, contacts, and knowledge regardless of the other parent.
# For attitudes the argument is much weaker. An attitude is not a resource
# that the household draws on; children are exposed to both parents, so a
# mean would represent the climate at home better than a maximum.
# The mother's education is often the stronger predictor of socialisation
# outcomes, which the maximum ignores completely.



4. Distance between home and work

home_work <- read_dta("data/home_work.dta")
# adjust the file name if the dataset is stored in a different format


home_work <- home_work |>
  mutate(
    d = sqrt((home_x - work_x)^2 + (home_y - work_y)^2),
    d_km = round(d)
  )
# Pythagoras' theorem on a flat earth
# the coordinates are rounded to whole kilometres, so reporting d to the
# nearest kilometre is the finest unit that is still meaningful

hin95_birthdates <- read_dta("data/hin95_birthdates.dta")

hin95_birthdates <- hin95_birthdates |>

# the remainder after dividing by 10000 is mmyy; dividing that by 100 leaves the month

7. Postcodes and city names

hin95_naw <- read_dta("data/hin95_naw.dta")
# adjust the file name if the dataset is stored in a different format

Extract the numeric part of the postcode.

hin95_naw <- hin95_naw |>
  mutate(
    pcode_str = str_sub(postcode, 1, 4),
    npcode = as.numeric(pcode_str)
  )
# first take the substring "1234", which is still a string
# then convert that string to the number 1234

Check the conversion.

hin95_naw |>
  select(postcode, pcode_str, npcode) |>
  slice(1:10)

# A tibble: 10 × 3
   postcode pcode_str npcode
   <chr>    <chr>      <dbl>
 1 2742 CL  2742        2742
 2 3014 AH  3014        3014
 3 6006 JL  6006        6006
 4 6511 EC  6511        6511
 5 3817 AR  3817        3817
 6 6658 XJ  6658        6658
 7 5912 CD  5912        5912
 8 3522 CE  3522        3522
 9 1077 ZD  1077        1077
10 3084 RN  3084        3084

# pcode_str is left-aligned text, npcode is a right-aligned number


hin95_naw |>
  summarise(
    mean_npcode = mean(npcode, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

# A tibble: 1 × 1
  mean_npcode
        <dbl>
1       4639.

# the mean of npcode


# How should this mean be interpreted?
#
# Strictly speaking it should not be interpreted at all. Postcodes are
# labels, not quantities: the difference between 1000 and 2000 does not
# measure anything. Dutch postcodes are assigned roughly by region, so the
# mean says something vague about the geographic centre of gravity of the
# sample, but it is not a meaningful average of anything the respondents
# have. The variable is useful for merging with regional data, not as a
# variable in an analysis.

Convert the city name into a factor.

hin95_naw <- hin95_naw |>
  mutate(
    plaats_f = factor(plaats)
  )
# factor() creates the categories automatically from the distinct values
# the levels are sorted alphabetically by default

Check the result.

nlevels(hin95_naw$plaats_f)

[1] 273

# the number of distinct cities


hin95_naw |>
  count(plaats_f, sort = TRUE) |>
  slice(1:10)

Note that identical cities spelled differently, or with leading or trailing spaces, become separate levels. Cleaning the string first avoids this.

hin95_naw |>
  mutate(
    plaats_clean = factor(str_to_upper(str_trim(plaats)))
  ) |>
  summarise(
    levels_raw = nlevels(factor(plaats)),
    levels_clean = nlevels(plaats_clean)
  )

# A tibble: 1 × 2
  levels_raw levels_clean
       <int>        <int>
1        273          273

# if the two counts differ, the raw variable contained spelling inconsistencies

title: Documenting data
text: In this short section you will learn about the following basic tasks:

title: Documenting data
text:
R
Learn the following R commands to document the data, variables, and values:



Function
Description




rename()
Rename variables


mutate()
Modify or create variables


factor()
Convert a variable to a factor


na_if()
Change a specific value to NA


replace_na()
Replace NA with a specific value


relocate()
Change the order of variables



Rename variables:

data <- data |> 
  rename(educ = v101) 
# rename v101 to educ

data <- data |> 
  rename(sex = v1, edu = v2) 
# rename multiple variables

Convert a categorical variable to a factor:

data <- data |>
  mutate(
    sex = factor(
      sex,
      levels = c(1, 2),
      labels = c("male", "female")
    )
  )
# assign meaningful labels to categories

Code missing values:

data <- data |> 
  mutate(educ = na_if(educ, 99)) 
# change the value 99 to NA 

data <- data |> mutate(across(c(educ, feduc), ~ na_if(.x, 9))) 
# change the value 9 to NA in educ and feduc

Replace missing values with a numeric code:

data <- data |> 
  mutate(educ = replace_na(educ, 99)) 
# change NA to 99

Change the order of variables:

data <- data |> 
  relocate(hrespnr, sex, age, edu) 
# put these variables first 

Be careful when replacing missing values with numeric codes such as 99. In R, missing values should usually be coded as NA. Numeric missing-value codes can easily be treated as real values in analyses if they are not recoded properly.

title: Documenting data
text:
Assignments
See dh_doc.Rmd for solutions.
In these assignments we use the dataset sbs399_unlabeled.dta.

Rename the variable hrespnr to hid and the variable hrinc to hinc in one command.
The variable sex is coded numerically. Convert sex into a factor with meaningful labels. Use male and female as category labels.
The variables sexrol1 and sexrol2 measure family attitudes. Convert both variables into factors with the following category labels:

fully disagree
slightly disagree
indifferent
slightly agree
fully agree

title: Documenting data
text:
Answers

1. Rename the variable hrespnr to hid and the variable hrinc to hinc in one command.

data <- data |>
  rename(
    hid = hrespnr,
    hinc = hrinc
  )



2. The variable sex is coded numerically. Convert sex into a factor with meaningful labels. Use male and female as category labels.

data <- data |>
  mutate(
    sex = factor(
      sex,
      levels = c(1, 2),
      labels = c("male", "female")
    )
  )



3. The variables sexrol1 and sexrol2 measure family attitudes. Convert both variables into factors with the following category labels: fully disagree, slightly disagree, indifferent, slightly agree, fully agree.

data <- data |>
  mutate(
    sexrol1 = factor(
      sexrol1,
      levels = c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5),
      labels = c(
        "fully disagree",
        "slightly disagree",
        "indifferent",
        "slightly agree",
        "fully agree"
      )
    ),
    sexrol2 = factor(
      sexrol2,
      levels = c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5),
      labels = c(
        "fully disagree",
        "slightly disagree",
        "indifferent",
        "slightly agree",
        "fully agree"
      )
    )
  )

title: Aggregating data
text:
In this chapter you learn about the two related tasks:
To illustrate, consider the following pet dataset with 5 pupils with respondent identifier id, from 2 school classes identified by the variable class, recording the father’s education of the pupil in the variable fedu.
The dataset with class-level summary statistics should contain 2 cases, one for each class, with the mean of fedu in the respective classes, new variable mn_fedu, and the number of observations, new variable n, in each class.
The original individual-level dataset enriched with class-level summary statistics should read:
Thus, the variable mn_fedu records contextual, class-level, information in de-aggregated form: the mean education of the parents in a pupil’s class is treated as an individual attribute.

title: Aggregating data
text:
R
In this part you need to study the following R functions:



Function
Description




summarise()
Create a dataset with summary statistics


mutate()
Add new variables to the existing dataset


.by
Apply summarise() or mutate() within groups


n()
Count the number of observations in a group


mean()
Compute group means


min()
Compute group minimums


max()
Compute group maximums



We present a short code fragment to accomplish the data manipulation described in the preamble.
Add the mean of fedu by class as a variable, N = 5:

data <- data |>
  mutate(
    mn_fedu = mean(fedu, na.rm = TRUE),
    .by = class
  )

Add variable nclass: number of observations in each class:

data <- data |>
  mutate(
    nclass = n(),
    .by = class
  )

Create a N = 2 contextual dataset with the N and mean of fedu, grouped by class:

class_data <- data |>
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    mn_fedu = mean(fedu, na.rm = TRUE),
    .by = class
  )

title: Aggregating data
text:
Assignments
See dh_aggregate_assignments.Rmd for solutions.

1. People nested within neighborhoods within cities
We consider a simple synthetic dataset ex_aggr.dta of people nested within neighborhoods nested within cities.
city city code
neighb neighborhood code
employ employment status, 1 = employed, 0 = unemployed
ethnic 1 = native Dutch; 2 = western immigrant; 3 = nonwestern immigrant

Create a separate dataset recording the fractions of unemployed and the ethnic composition of cities, i.e., the fractions of native Dutch, western immigrants, and nonwestern immigrants.
Add variables to the original dataset with the fractions, or percentages, of unemployed and the ethnic composition of the neighborhood, i.e., the fractions, or percentages, of Dutch, western, and nonwestern people in the neighborhood. Briefly consider how to also add the information aggregated at the city level.
Add a variable representing the fraction, or percentage, of ethnic ingroup in the neighborhood.



2. Education within couples
Use hin95_ext.dta. The dataset contains data on couples, married or cohabiting, indicated by the household identifier hrespnr.

Add a variable for the mean education of the household. Thus, this variable should have the same value for both partners.
Add a variable for the minimum education of the household. Add a variable for the maximum education of the household.
Add a variable recording the absolute difference of the levels of education of husband and wife.

title: Creating a system file from raw data
text:
In this part you learn about reading raw data into R. Raw data are often stored as text files that can be opened using a simple text editor. Typically the data are in the form of a data matrix in which the rows are cases, columns are variables, and values are separated by commas, tabs, or spaces.
In modern R workflows, raw data are usually read from files such as CSV, tab-delimited text files, Excel files, or Stata files. Occasionally, it is also useful to create a small dataset manually in R, for example for examples, tests, or teaching.

title: Creating a system file from raw data
text:
R
In this part you need to learn and read about the following R functions:



Function
Description




read_csv()
Read comma-separated text data


read_tsv()
Read tab-separated text data


read_table()
Read whitespace-separated text data


read_dta()
Read a Stata dataset


write_csv()
Save data as a CSV file


write_rds()
Save data as an R object


tribble()
Manually create a small dataset


View()
Inspect a dataset in RStudio



Examples:
Read a CSV file:

library(readr)
data <- read_csv("data/mydata.csv")

Read a tab-delimited text file:

data <- read_tsv("data/mydata.txt")

Read a whitespace-separated text file:

data <- read_table("data/mydata.dat")

Read a Stata dataset:

library(haven)
data <- read_dta("data/mydata.dta")

Create a small dataset manually:

library(tibble)
data <- tribble(
  ~hrespnr, ~city,        ~female, ~edu,
  101,      "Amsterdam",  1,       3,
  103,      "Den Haag",   0,       5,
  107,      "Rotterdam",  0,       2,
  109,      "Utrecht",    1,       3
)

Inspect the dataset:

View(data)

Save the dataset as a CSV file:

write_csv(data, "data/mydata.csv")

Save the dataset as an R object:

write_rds(data, "data/mydata.rds")

text:
Assignments

1. Manual entering data
We want to create an R dataset with the following variables:



hrespnr
city

Do this in two ways.
First, create the dataset manually in R using tribble().
Second, create the same dataset as a CSV file, save it in your data/ folder, and read it into R using read_csv().
Save both newly created datasets.

title: Creating a system file from raw data
text:
Answers
Make sure this file is in the same R Project as the data folder. Use relative file paths, not full paths to your computer.

library(tidyverse)

✖ dplyr::lag()    masks stats::lag()
ℹ Use the conflicted package (<http://conflicted.r-lib.org/>) to force all conflicts to become errors



1. Manual entering data
Enter the data by hand with tribble().

mydata <- tribble(
  ~hrespnr, ~city,        ~female, ~edu,
  101,      "Amsterdam",  1,       3,
  103,      "Den Haag",   0,       5,
  107,      "Rotterdam",  0,       2,
  109,      "Utrecht",    1,       3
)

mydata

# A tibble: 4 × 4
  hrespnr city      female   edu
    <dbl> <chr>      <dbl> <dbl>
1     101 Amsterdam      1     3
2     103 Den Haag       0     5
3     107 Rotterdam      0     2
4     109 Utrecht        1     3

# tribble() lays the data out row by row, so the code looks like the table
# the column names are preceded by a tilde

Check what R made of the variable types.

glimpse(mydata)

Rows: 4
Columns: 4
$ hrespnr <dbl> 101, 103, 107, 109
$ city    <chr> "Amsterdam", "Den Haag", "Rotterdam", "Utrecht"
$ female  <dbl> 1, 0, 0, 1
$ edu     <dbl> 3, 5, 2, 3

# city is a character variable; the other three are numeric (dbl)
# note that hrespnr and female are identifiers and codes, not quantities,
# even though R stores them as numbers

Save this version.

write_rds(mydata, "data/mydata_tribble.rds")
# .rds keeps the object exactly as it is, including variable types

Now build the same dataset as a CSV file. Writing the file from R is the reproducible way to do it; you could equally well type it in a text editor and save it as data/mydata.csv.

csv_text <- "hrespnr,city,female,edu
101,Amsterdam,1,3
103,Den Haag,0,5
107,Rotterdam,0,2
109,Utrecht,1,3
"

write_file(csv_text, "data/mydata.csv")
# the first line holds the variable names, each following line is one case
# values are separated by commas, without spaces after them

Look at the file as plain text, the way a text editor would show it.

read_file("data/mydata.csv") |>
  cat()

hrespnr,city,female,edu
101,Amsterdam,1,3
103,Den Haag,0,5
107,Rotterdam,0,2
109,Utrecht,1,3

# a CSV file is just text: no formatting, no types, only characters

Read the file back into R.

mydata_csv <- read_csv("data/mydata.csv")

Rows: 4 Columns: 4
── Column specification ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Delimiter: ","
chr (1): city
dbl (3): hrespnr, female, edu

ℹ Use `spec()` to retrieve the full column specification for this data.
ℹ Specify the column types or set `show_col_types = FALSE` to quiet this message.

mydata_csv

# A tibble: 4 × 4
  hrespnr city      female   edu
    <dbl> <chr>      <dbl> <dbl>
1     101 Amsterdam      1     3
2     103 Den Haag       0     5
3     107 Rotterdam      0     2
4     109 Utrecht        1     3

# read_csv() reports which type it guessed for each column

Verify that both routes produced the same dataset.

all.equal(mydata, mydata_csv)

[1] "Attributes: < Names: 1 string mismatch >"                                              
[2] "Attributes: < Length mismatch: comparison on first 2 components >"                     
[3] "Attributes: < Component \"class\": Lengths (3, 4) differ (string compare on first 3) >"
[4] "Attributes: < Component \"class\": 3 string mismatches >"                              
[5] "Attributes: < Component 2: Modes: numeric, externalptr >"                              
[6] "Attributes: < Component 2: Lengths: 4, 1 >"                                            
[7] "Attributes: < Component 2: target is numeric, current is externalptr >"                

# TRUE means the two datasets are identical in content and types

Save the version read from CSV.

write_rds(mydata_csv, "data/mydata_csv.rds")

A remark on types. read_csv() guesses the type of each column from its contents, whereas tribble() takes the types from what you typed. Here both give the same result, but a guess can go wrong: an identifier with leading zeros, such as a postcode 0234, would be read as the number 234. You can override the guess.

mydata_typed <- read_csv(
  "data/mydata.csv",
  col_types = cols(
    hrespnr = col_character(),
    city = col_character(),
    female = col_double(),
    edu = col_double()
  )
)

glimpse(mydata_typed)

Rows: 4
Columns: 4
$ hrespnr <chr> "101", "103", "107", "109"
$ city    <chr> "Amsterdam", "Den Haag", "Rotterdam", "Utrecht"
$ female  <dbl> 1, 0, 0, 1
$ edu     <dbl> 3, 5, 2, 3

# hrespnr is now text, which is what an identifier really is

Finally, a note on why .rds and .csv are both useful. A CSV file can be opened by any program and read by anyone, but it stores only text and loses the variable types. An .rds file preserves the R object exactly, but only R can read it.

list.files("data", pattern = "^mydata")

[1] "mydata.csv"         "mydata_csv.rds"     "mydata_tribble.rds"

title: Adding cases and variables
text:
In this chapter, you will learn about how to combine different datasets:
We will elaborate on and illustrate these tasks with simple examples. As a first example, you organize an international data collection, where all countries use the same questionnaire. You obtain datasets from the Netherlands, from the UK, etc. The datasets contain (largely) the same variables. You want to make one dataset of these country datasets, with an additional variable country recording the data source. As a second example, we consider that the two files to be combined contain different variables. We need to distinguish two cases:
A crucial concept in merging is a key. A key comprises one or more variables used to match observations from the two datasets. In the example of 1:1 merging, the key is likely a subject identifier. In the example on n:1 merging, the key is the city identifier. The key variable or variables should occur in both datasets. In R, key variables do not necessarily need to have the same name in both datasets, but using the same name is usually clearer and less error-prone.
PS: The first type of merge is also possible without a key variable or key variables, and strictly on sequential order of the files: the first record of file A with the first record of file B, the second record of file A with the second record of file B, etc. This type of merging is very error prone. We urge you never to merge without keys.
Task 1. As a pet example of adding cases, we consider two datasets. The dataset world95_oecd_eu describes the population size of a selection of 4 European OECD members:
while world95_oecd_extra describes a selection of 3 non-European OECD members:
The first task that we want you to master is to create a new dataset that contains all 7 OECD countries:
Task 2. As a pet example of 1:1 merging, we consider two datasets with characteristics of a collection of countries, namely the population size, dataset world95_3_pop:
and religion in dataset world95_3_rel:
Note that the second dataset does not contain Armenia; Armenia is missing in the second dataset. As a second task we will address the creation of the 1:1 merged combined dataset that contains two characteristics of all countries involved:
Note that in the combined dataset, Armenia is included, but the religion of Armenia is missing.
Task 3. A paradigmatic example of n:1 merging involves adding contextual data to information on individual subjects. We consider a pet example with 4 individuals from various countries:
A separate file contains characteristics of various countries:
Note that the individual dataset contains a subject from the Netherlands, but the population size of the Netherlands is not available. Moreover, we have contextual information about Argentina, but no subject from Argentina. As your third task, you have to learn how to create the n:1 merge of the datasets, adding country properties to the individual data:
Task 4. We want to analyze school choice by parents. In the pet example we have 4 parents each of whom can choose between 3 schools. We want to construct a dataset that consists of combinations of parents and schools.

title: Adding cases and variables
text:
R
You should read about the following R functions:



Function
Description




bind_rows()
Append datasets, add cases


left_join()
Merge datasets, add variables



We present an R snippet for the four tasks:

Add cases

world95_oecd_eu
world95_oecd_extra

oecd <- bind_rows(
  world95_oecd_eu,
  world95_oecd_extra
)

oecd



1:1 merge

world95_3_pop
world95_3_rel

countries <- world95_3_pop |>
  left_join(
    world95_3_rel,
    by = "country"
  )

countries



n:1 merge

merge_indiv
world95_3_pop

individuals <- merge_indiv |>
  left_join(
    world95_3_pop,
    by = "country"
  )

individuals



All combinations of parents and schools

schools <- schools |>
  rename(
    school_public = public
  ) |>
  mutate(join_key = 1)

parents <- parents |>
  rename(
    pstatus = status,
    pneigh = neighb,
    pchoice = choice
  ) |>
  mutate(join_key = 1)

pairs <- parents |>
  left_join(
    schools,
    by = "join_key"
  ) |>
  select(-join_key)

pairs

Some notes on combining datasets

To append datasets, make sure that corresponding variables in both datasets have the same names, and are coded in the same way. For example, you do not want sex to be coded 0 = male and 1 = female in one dataset, and 0 = female and 1 = male in the other.
Issues to consider with key variables for merging:
Make sure that the keys are coded identically in both datasets. If you merge on country, the country code should obviously refer to the same country in both datasets.
In a 1:1 merge, make sure to always use a key, e.g., the respondent number. Do not rely on the assumption that the first observation in one dataset corresponds with the first observation in the other dataset.
R allows composite keys for merging, i.e., the key may consist of multiple variables, e.g., country and year.
Do not merge on keys with missing values, unless you really know what you are doing.
left_join() keeps all observations from the first dataset and adds matching information from the second dataset. Observations in the first dataset without a match receive NA on the variables from the second dataset.
As always: Do not assume that combining files was successful if R does not complain. Check the number of observations. Check the variables. Check values. Check everything.

title: Adding cases and variables
text:
Assignments

1. Synthetic Eurobarometer data
The datasets eurobaro2000_ge, eurobaro2000_nl, and eurobaro2000_uk contain subsets of the Eurobarometer 2000 data, with small selections of respondents from Germany, the Netherlands, and the United Kingdom. These datasets comprise demographic information of respondents, sex and age, and their trust in two institutions of the European Union, the EU commission, tcomm, and the EU parliament, tparl, recorded using 5 point scales. Use bind_rows() to append these three datasets to create one dataset eb2000 for the three countries, adding a string variable country recording the data source. Add a year variable that includes the value 2000.
The datasets eurobaro2002 and eurobaro2004 similarly contain Eurobarometer data for the same three countries for the years 2002 and 2004. We want you to combine these two datasets with eb2000. However, there are some complications that you have to deal with.

the variable country in 2002: The United Kingdom is not abbreviated to uk as in 2000.
the variable country in 2004: It is a labelled numeric variable, not a string variable.
the variable sex in 2002: The meaning of 1 and 2 are reversed.
in 2002 and 2004, trust was also measured for the European Court of Law.
in 2004, trust was measured on a binary scale, 0 = no and 1 = yes, rather than on the 5 point scale used in 2000 and 2002.

We also have two contextual datasets. eudata contains the population size, in September 2012, ignore the mismatch, of these EU countries. The dataset euydata describes the GDP in some EU countries in the years 2000 to 2004, rounded in 1000 EUR units. Enrich the individual data with these two contextual datasets using left_join().


2. Add cases: appending datasets
In this assignment we consider how to combine observations from multiple files. For instance, data entry from paper questionnaires is performed by different people, yielding different datasets with the same variables for different subjects.

As this exercise is meant to develop your computer skills, we are going to generate two disjoint sets of records ourselves.

Load sbs399. Select the men. Save the data as sbs399m.
Reload sbs399. This time select the women. Save the data as sbs399f.


To reconstruct the full dataset sbs399 from these two partial datasets on women and men respectively, append the files using bind_rows().

Now do a more complicated append of the files involving different subjects and partially different variables. To simulate this, repeat steps 1 and 2, but now you delete some variables from the male file and some other variables from the female file. Append the files using bind_rows(). How does R deal with the variables that appear in one dataset, but not in the other?



3. 1:1 merge: adding variables
In this assignment, we consider how to combine multiple files that comprise different variables for the same subjects. In real life, this may for instance occur in a panel study, in which data from different waves are stored in separate files. We require you create such datasets for training purposes.

Use isbs399. This is a variant of sbs399 in which we excluded same-sex households. If you want to, you may consider constructing isbs399 from sbs399 yourself. This dataset comprises couples nested in households and singles. Respondents are identified with hrespnr. Save two subsets of isbs399, one with the variables hrespnr, hrespnr, sex, ybirth, and age; the other with hrespnr, hrespnr, sex, fage, and fpres.
Match the two files you just created, using hrespnr as the key and left_join(). Ascertain that the merged file is correct.
Now create the two subsets of isbs399 again, excluding the first observation in the first file, and the second observation in the second file. Merge again on hrespnr using left_join(). Inspect the first two observations. What do you conclude?
Merge the two datasets once more, this time matching on hrespnr. Why does it not work? Yes, hrespnr does not uniquely identify observations. The pair hrespnr and sex does uniquely identify subjects, and so they make a valid composite key. Merge on the pair hrespnr and sex, and convince yourself that this leads to the same result as merging on hrespnr.



4. n:1 merge: contextual enrichment
In this assignment we consider how to enrich an individual level dataset with contextual data. The dataset sbs399 contains information on individuals nested in couples or households, identified by the household identifier hrespnr. The dataset hin95_house provides properties of the couple’s house, ownership, number of rooms, etc. Thus, hin95_house also contains the household identifier.
Merge sbs399 and hin95_house on hrespnr using left_join().


5. Cities and regions
We consider a partially synthetic example with three datasets. The dataset mm_hn95data contains information about households, including the city of residence, and the cities in which the husband and wife work. The second dataset mm_cities contains information about cities, including the region to which the city belongs. The third dataset mm_regions contains information about regions. For your convenience, we list the variables in the three datasets.
mm_hn95data
hhid household id
city city of residence
hhinc household income

Continuing with this merged dataset, now add the economic growth in the region of residence from the dataset mm_regions using left_join().
We start again with the unmodified dataset mm_hn95data. This dataset contains the ids of three cities relevant to the households: the city in which they live, city, the city in which the husband works, hwcity, and the city in which the wife works, wwcity. We want you to merge in information about each of the cities, adding three variables, e.g., named res_inhabit, hwcity_inhabit, and wwcity_inhabit, for the number of inhabitants in each of the cities. Use left_join() multiple times.



6. Distance between home and work
In the chapter on functions, we computed the straight line distance between a subject’s home and work address. In this stylized example, we consider two small datasets.     country = as.character(as_factor(country)),
    year = 2004

The trust scales are the real problem. Trust measured on a 5 point scale and trust measured as yes/no are not the same variable, and stacking them into one column would produce a variable whose meaning depends on the year.

# Three defensible options:
#
# 1. Keep them apart. Rename the 2004 items to tcomm_bin, tparl_bin, tcourt_bin
#    so that no column ever mixes the two scales. Honest, but you cannot
#    analyse trust over all three years in one model.
#
# 2. Dichotomise 2000 and 2002 to match 2004. Collapse the 5 point scale into
#    trust yes/no. This throws away detail, but makes all three years
#    comparable on the coarser scale.
#
# 3. Keep both: one column per scale, plus a harmonised binary column that is
#    filled for every year. This is what we do below, because it preserves the
#    original data and still allows a pooled analysis.
#
# What you should NOT do is put 1-5 and 0-1 values in the same column.

Decide where the 5 point scale is split. This is a substantive choice, so state it explicitly.

table(eb2000$tcomm, useNA = "ifany")


2 3 4 5 
1 2 2 1 

# inspect the 5 point distribution before choosing a cut point
# we treat 4 and 5 as "trust", assuming higher values mean more trust
# reverse this if your codebook says otherwise


eb2000 <- eb2000 |>
  mutate(across(c(tcomm, tparl), \(x) if_else(x >= 4, 1, 0), .names = "{.col}_bin"))

eb2002 <- eb2002 |>
  mutate(across(c(tcomm, tparl, tcourt), \(x) if_else(x >= 4, 1, 0), .names = "{.col}_bin"))

eb2004 <- eb2004 |>
  rename(tcomm_bin = tcomm, tparl_bin = tparl, tcourt_bin = tcourt)
# after this, tcomm/tparl/tcourt hold the 5 point scale where it exists,

# at the cost of losing two variables entirely



3. 1:1 merge: adding variables
Create two subsets with different variables for the same respondents.

part_a <- isbs399 |>
  select(hrespnr, sex, ybirth, age)

part_b <- isbs399 |>
  select(hrespnr, hrespnr, sex, fage, fpres)

nrow(part_a)

[1] 3330

nrow(part_b)

[1] 3330

n_distinct(isbs399$hrespnr) == nrow(isbs399)

[1] FALSE

# hrespnr should uniquely identify a respondent

Merge on hrespnr.

merged <- part_a |>
  left_join(
    part_b |> select(hrespnr, fage, fpres),
    by = "hrespnr"
  )

Warning in left_join(part_a, select(part_b, hrespnr, fage, fpres), by = "hrespnr"): Detected an unexpected many-to-many relationship between `x` and `y`.
ℹ Row 2 of `x` matches multiple rows in `y`.
ℹ Row 2 of `y` matches multiple rows in `x`.
ℹ If a many-to-many relationship is expected, set `relationship =
  "many-to-many"` to silence this warning.

nrow(merged)

[1] 6372

names(merged)

[1] "hrespnr" "sex"     "ybirth"  "age"     "fage"    "fpres"  

# selecting only the key and the new variables from part_b avoids duplicate
# columns such as hrespnr.x and hrespnr.y

Verify the merge.

merged |>
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    missing_fage = sum(is.na(fage)),
    missing_fpres = sum(is.na(fpres))
  )

# A tibble: 1 × 3
      n missing_fage missing_fpres
  <int>        <int>         <int>
1  6372            0             0

# no rows added, no unexpected missing values


all.equal(
  merged |> arrange(hrespnr) |> select(hrespnr, ybirth, fage),
  isbs399 |> arrange(hrespnr) |> select(hrespnr, ybirth, fage)
)

[1] "Attributes: < Component \"row.names\": Numeric: lengths (6372, 3330) differ >"
[2] "Component \"hrespnr\": Numeric: lengths (6372, 3330) differ"                  
[3] "Component \"ybirth\": Numeric: lengths (6372, 3330) differ"                   
[4] "Component \"fage\": Numeric: lengths (6372, 3330) differ"                     

# the merged file reproduces the original variables exactly

Now drop one observation from each file and merge again.

part_a2 <- part_a |> slice(-1)
part_b2 <- part_b |> slice(-2)

merged2 <- part_a2 |>
  left_join(
    part_b2 |> select(hrespnr, fage, fpres),
    by = "hrespnr"
  )

Warning in left_join(part_a2, select(part_b2, hrespnr, fage, fpres), by = "hrespnr"): Detected an unexpected many-to-many relationship between `x` and `y`.
ℹ Row 3 of `x` matches multiple rows in `y`.
ℹ Row 2 of `y` matches multiple rows in `x`.
ℹ If a many-to-many relationship is expected, set `relationship =
  "many-to-many"` to silence this warning.

merged2 |>
  slice(1:2)

# A tibble: 2 × 6
  hrespnr sex       ybirth   age  fage fpres
    <dbl> <dbl+lbl>  <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
1   11002 1 [woman]     69    26    27    22
2   11002 0 [man]       62    33    27    22



nrow(part_a2)

[1] 3329

nrow(merged2)

[1] 6369

sum(is.na(merged2$fage))

[1] 0

# left_join() keeps every row of the left dataset
# the respondent dropped from part_b2 survives, but with NA on fage and fpres
# the respondent dropped from part_a2 disappears entirely


# What do you conclude?
#
# The result depends on which dataset you start from. left_join() is not
# symmetric: rows unmatched on the left are kept with NA, rows unmatched on
# the right are silently discarded.
#
# Crucially, the merge is still correct: because we joined on a key, every
# respondent was matched to their own record. Had we merged on position
# instead, dropping one row from each file by different amounts would have
# shifted the files against each other and paired the wrong people, without
# any error message at all. That is the argument for always using a key.


# full_join() keeps unmatched rows from both sides, which makes the
# asymmetry visible:

full_join(
  part_a2,
  part_b2 |> select(hrespnr, fage, fpres),
  by = "hrespnr"
) |>
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    only_in_a = sum(is.na(fage)),
    only_in_b = sum(is.na(age))
  )

Warning in full_join(part_a2, select(part_b2, hrespnr, fage, fpres), by = "hrespnr"): Detected an unexpected many-to-many relationship between `x` and `y`.
ℹ Row 3 of `x` matches multiple rows in `y`.
ℹ Row 2 of `y` matches multiple rows in `x`.
ℹ If a many-to-many relationship is expected, set `relationship =
  "many-to-many"` to silence this warning.


# A tibble: 1 × 3
      n only_in_a only_in_b
  <int>     <int>     <int>
1  6370         0         1


Merge on hrespnr instead.

merged_wrong <- part_a |>
  left_join(
    part_b |> select(hrespnr, fage, fpres),
    by = "hrespnr",
    relationship = "many-to-many"
  )

nrow(part_a)

[1] 3330

nrow(merged_wrong)

[1] 6372

# the number of rows explodes


# Why does it not work?
#
# hrespnr identifies a household, not a person. A two-person household has
# two records on each side, so every record on the left matches both records
# on the right: 2 x 2 = 4 rows instead of 2. Each partner is paired with the
# other partner's father as well as with their own.
#
# Without relationship = "many-to-many", dplyr raises a warning about an
# unexpected many-to-many relationship. That warning is the single most
# useful diagnostic in this whole chapter: it means your key is not what you
# thought it was.

Use the composite key hrespnr and sex.

merged_composite <- part_a |>
  left_join(
    part_b |> select(hrespnr, sex, fage, fpres),
    by = c("hrespnr", "sex")
  )

nrow(merged_composite)

[1] 3330

nrow(merged)

[1] 6372

# the composite key restores a one-to-one match


all.equal(
  merged |> arrange(hrespnr) |> select(hrespnr, fage, fpres),
  merged_composite |> arrange(hrespnr) |> select(hrespnr, fage, fpres)
)

[1] "Attributes: < Component \"row.names\": Numeric: lengths (6372, 3330) differ >"
[2] "Component \"hrespnr\": Numeric: lengths (6372, 3330) differ"                  
[3] "Component \"fage\": Numeric: lengths (6372, 3330) differ"                     
[4] "Component \"fpres\": Numeric: lengths (6372, 3330) differ"                    

# merging on hrespnr + sex gives the same result as merging on hrespnr
# this works only because isbs399 excludes same-sex households: in a same-sex
# couple both partners share hrespnr AND sex, and the key would fail again



4. n:1 merge: contextual enrichment

nrow(sbs399)

[1] 3350

nrow(hin95_house)

[1] 1821

n_distinct(hin95_house$hrespnr) == nrow(hin95_house)

[1] TRUE

  left_join(hin95_house, by = "hrespnr")

nrow(sbs399)

[1] 3350

nrow(sbs399_house)

[1] 3350

sbs399_house |>
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    matched = sum(!is.na(rooms)),
    unmatched = sum(is.na(rooms))

# A tibble: 1 × 3
      n matched unmatched
  <int>   <int>     <int>
1  3350    3334        16

# replace rooms by any variable that comes from hin95_house
# unmatched households are those present in sbs399 but absent from hin95_house


setdiff(unique(sbs399$hrespnr), unique(hin95_house$hrespnr)) |> length()

[1] 0

setdiff(unique(hin95_house$hrespnr), unique(sbs399$hrespnr)) |> length()

[1] 2

# households in the individual data without house information, and
# house records for households that contain no respondents
# the second group is dropped by left_join(), which is usually what you want


sbs399_house |>
  select(hrespnr, sex, age, rooms) |>
  arrange(hrespnr) |>
  slice(1:6)

5. Cities and regions
Merge the city properties into the household data.

names(mm_hn95data)

 [1] "hhid"     "city"     "hhinc"    "nkids"    "hrace"    "hwcity"  
 [7] "wrace"    "wwcity"   "religion" "vchurch" 

names(mm_cities)

[1] "cityid"  "inhabit" "region"  "jobs"    "vacant" 

# the key variables have different names: city on the left, cityid on the right


n_distinct(mm_cities$cityid) == nrow(mm_cities)

[1] TRUE

# the city file must be unique on cityid for an n:1 merge


hh_city <- mm_hn95data |>
  left_join(mm_cities, by = c("city" = "cityid"))

nrow(mm_hn95data)

[1] 1534

nrow(hh_city)

[1] 1534

names(hh_city)

 [7] "wrace"    "wwcity"   "religion" "vchurch"  "inhabit"  "region"  
[13] "jobs"     "vacant"

# the left-hand name is kept in the result


hh_city |>
  summarise(
    unmatched = sum(is.na(inhabit))
  )

# A tibble: 1 × 1
  unmatched
      <int>
1       196

# households living in a city that is absent from mm_cities

Add the regional data.

n_distinct(mm_regions$regid) == nrow(mm_regions)

[1] TRUE

hh_city_region <- hh_city |>
  left_join(mm_regions, by = c("region" = "regid"))

nrow(hh_city_region)

names(hh_city_region)

[13] "jobs"     "vacant"   "growth"

# this is a chain of n:1 merges: households in cities in regions

# a household can fail to match at either level

Merge city information three times, for the city of residence and both work cities.

mm_hn95data_3 <- mm_hn95data |>
  left_join(
    mm_cities |> select(cityid, res_inhabit = inhabit),
    by = c("city" = "cityid")

6. Distance between home and work
Create the two datasets by hand.

subjects <- tribble(
  ~id,  ~edu, ~hcity, ~wcity,
  101,  2,    2,      4,
  102,  4,    3,      3,
  109,  3,    1,      3,
  115,  2,    4,      2,
  121,  1,    3,      NA
)

cities <- tribble(
  ~city, ~x,  ~y,
  1,     5,   -5,
  2,     30,  19,
  3,     -18, 50,
  4,     10,  0,
  5,     -3,  1
)

subjects

# A tibble: 5 × 4
     id   edu hcity wcity
  <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
1   101     2     2     4
2   102     4     3     3
3   109     3     1     3
4   115     2     4     2
5   121     1     3    NA

cities

# A tibble: 5 × 3
   city     x     y
  <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
1     1     5    -5
2     2    30    19
3     3   -18    50
4     4    10     0
5     5    -3     1


Merge the coordinates twice, once for the home city and once for the work city.

subjects_xy <- subjects |>
  left_join(
    cities |> select(city, hx = x, hy = y),
    by = c("hcity" = "city")
  ) |>
  left_join(
    cities |> select(city, wx = x, wy = y),
    by = c("wcity" = "city")
  )

subjects_xy

# A tibble: 5 × 8
     id   edu hcity wcity    hx    hy    wx    wy
  <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
1   101     2     2     4    30    19    10     0
2   102     4     3     3   -18    50   -18    50
3   109     3     1     3     5    -5   -18    50
4   115     2     4     2    10     0    30    19
5   121     1     3    NA   -18    50    NA    NA

# renaming the coordinates inside select() keeps the four columns apart

Compute the distance.

subjects_xy <- subjects_xy |>
  mutate(
    d = sqrt((hx - wx)^2 + (hy - wy)^2),
    d_km = round(d)
  )

subjects_xy |>
  select(id, hcity, wcity, hx, hy, wx, wy, d_km)

# A tibble: 5 × 8
     id hcity wcity    hx    hy    wx    wy  d_km
  <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
1   101     2     4    30    19    10     0    28
2   102     3     3   -18    50   -18    50     0
3   109     1     3     5    -5   -18    50    60
4   115     4     2    10     0    30    19    28
5   121     3    NA   -18    50    NA    NA    NA

# rounding to whole kilometres matches the precision of the coordinates


# Two cases are worth checking by hand:
#
# Subject 102 lives and works in city 3, so the distance is exactly 0.
# Subject 121 has no work city, so wcity is NA, the join produces NA
#   coordinates, and the distance is NA. That is the correct outcome: we
#   cannot compute a distance to an unknown location.
#
# Note that city 5 appears in no subject's record. left_join() simply
# ignores it, which is what we want: the city file is a lookup table, not a
# source of cases.


subjects_xy |>
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    computable = sum(!is.na(d_km)),
    mean_distance = mean(d_km, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

      n computable mean_distance
  <int>      <int>         <dbl>
1     5          4            29

title: Restructuring data
text:
We may present panel data, data on people indicated by id, for different years indicated by year, in long format:
or in wide format:
Be sure that you understand that these two datasets contain the same information, but only represent the information in a different way. One can translate one form into the other form. The variables inc and stat are said to be time-varying, while male is time-constant.
In this part you practice the R functions that automatically restructure data between long format and wide format. You need to learn about this because your data may be in one format, while the data management or statistical method you want to use requires the data to be in the other format.
For instance, multilevel analysis typically requires data to be in long format, e.g., measurements at different time points are stored in different rows, while structural equation modeling often requires wide data, e.g., measurements stored in different variables. In SaSR7 you will learn about these statistical methods. For now, we only introduce how to get the data into the correct format.

title: Restructuring data
text:
R
You should read about the following R functions:



Function
Description




pivot_longer()
Convert data from wide to long format


pivot_wider()
Convert data from long to wide format



Examples:
Restructure long to wide:

data_wide <- data_long |>
  pivot_wider(
    id_cols = c(id, male),
    names_from = year,
    values_from = c(inc, stat)
  )

Restructure wide to long:

data_long <- data_wide |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = -c(id, male),
    names_to = c(".value", "year"),
    names_pattern = "(.*)(\\d{4})"
  )

Note that pivot_longer() and pivot_wider() expect that variable names follow a consistent naming convention. In the example above, the variables are named using a prefix, inc and stat, followed by a year, 2000, 2001, and 2002, corresponding to the level of an index variable, here the year in which income and status were measured. If variables are not named consistently, you may need to rename them before restructuring the data.

title: Restructuring data
text:
Assignments
See dh_restructure_assignments.Rmd for solutions.

1. Longitudinal data in long and wide format
The dataset gpa2long.dta contains longitudinal data, taken from the book on multilevel analysis that we use in SaSR7, in long format.
student student identifier
occas measurement occasion, 0 = year 1 semester 1, 1 = year 1 semester 2, 2 = year 2 semester 1, 3 = year 2 semester 2, …
sex 0 = male, 1 = female
gpa grade-point average
job paid work hours per week
highgpa high school GPA
admitted admitted to university, 0 = no, 1 = yes, or missing

Which variables are time-constant and which are time-varying?
How many observations are there for student 1 and student 2?
Use pivot_wider() to convert the data to wide format using occas as the measurement occasion.
Which new variables are created?
How many observations does the wide dataset contain?
Convince yourself that information was preserved across the restructuring and that only the representation of the information changed.
Save the created dataset as gpa2wide.rds.
Load the wide dataset and use pivot_longer() to convert it back to long format.



2. Sex-specific country indicators
In this assignment, we use the World95 dataset. This dataset contains information for 109 countries. One observation corresponds to one country.
Some variables are sex-specific, e.g., the life expectancy for men and women (lifeexpm and lifeexpf respectively) and the literacy rates of men and women (lit_male and lit_female respectively). Other variables, e.g., populatn and density, are not sex-specific.
We want to create a dataset in which each country is represented by two observations, one describing the men and one describing the women of that country.
A new dummy variable female should describe whether a record pertains to women or men.
Thus, a new dataset has to be constructed with 2 × 109 = 218 observations, with at least the following variables:

country
female
population
density
lifeexp
lit

where population and density do not vary with gender, while lifeexp and lit do.

Which variables are gender-specific and which are not?
Rename variables if necessary so that they follow a consistent naming convention.
Use pivot_longer() to create the desired dataset.
Create a variable female.
Verify that the resulting dataset contains 218 observations.



3. Multilevel data in four formats
The synthetic dataset level4.dta contains multilevel data on three sex-role attitude measurements over time, 2002, 2004, and 2006, for both spouses of heterosexual couples.
hhid household id
iid individual id
urban urbanized
male
edu highest completed education, 1 to 10
year
att1 family value: man natural breadwinner
att2 family value: women are better with children
att3 family value: men and women equal decision makers
We say that the dataset level4 is in long-long-long-wide format for the key variables hhid, iid, year, and the not-yet-existing variable item.
The first term long refers to households, and reflects that households are stored in different observations identified by hhid.
The second term long refers to individuals, and reflects that partners are stored as separate observations identified by iid; the variable hhid allows linking people who form a couple.
The third long refers to time: measurements at different time points are stored in different observations, with time indicated by the variable year.
The final term wide specifies that the repeated attitude measurements are stored in different variables within an observation, not as different observations.
Make sure that you understand the data well.

Use pivot_longer() to convert the data from long-long-long-wide to long-long-long-long format, i.e., the items are stored in different observations rather than in different variables indexed by a new variable item.
Use pivot_wider() to convert the data from the original long-long-long-wide format to long-long-wide-wide format. Explain what an observation in this dataset represents.
Use pivot_wider() to convert the data from the original long-long-long-wide format to long-wide-wide-wide format, identifying individuals within households by male rather than by iid.


What happens, or would happen, if you identify people within households by iid?
Is using male as a person-within-household identifier correct if the data include same-sex households?

# variable names, types, and the first few values

Which variables are time-constant and which are time-varying?

gpa2long |>
  summarise(
    across(everything(), \(x) n_distinct(x)),
    .by = student

1     6     6     3     1       1        1

# for each variable, the largest number of distinct values found within a
# single student
# a maximum of 1 means the variable never changes within a student, so it is
# time-constant; a larger value means it is time-varying


# student  identifies the unit, so it is neither
# occas    is the time index, and varies by construction
# gpa      time-varying: the grade-point average changes each semester
# job      time-varying: working hours change between semesters
# sex      time-constant
# highgpa  time-constant: high school GPA is fixed before the study starts
# admitted time-constant: a single admission decision per student

How many observations are there for student 1 and student 2?

gpa2long |>
  filter(student %in% c(1, 2)) |>
  count(student)

# A tibble: 2 × 2
  student     n
    <dbl> <int>
1       1     6
2       2     6

# number of measurement occasions for the first two students


table(gpa2long$occas, useNA = "ifany")


  0   1   2   3   4   5 
200 200 200 200 200 200 

# the measurement occasions present in the data

Convert to wide format.

gpa2wide <- gpa2long |>
  pivot_wider(
    id_cols = c(student, sex, highgpa, admitted),
    names_from = occas,
    values_from = c(gpa, job),
    names_prefix = "t"
  )
# id_cols lists everything that identifies a student and does not vary over time
# values_from lists the time-varying variables
# names_prefix avoids variable names that start with a digit

Which new variables are created?

names(gpa2wide)

 [1] "student"  "sex"      "highgpa"  "admitted" "gpa_t0"   "gpa_t1"  
 [7] "gpa_t2"   "gpa_t3"   "gpa_t4"   "gpa_t5"   "job_t0"   "job_t1"  
[13] "job_t2"   "job_t3"   "job_t4"   "job_t5"  

# each time-varying variable is now split into one column per occasion

How many observations does the wide dataset contain?

nrow(gpa2wide)

[1] 200

n_distinct(gpa2long$student)

[1] 200

# the wide dataset has exactly one row per student

Was information preserved?

nrow(gpa2long)

[1] 1200

sum(!is.na(gpa2wide |> select(starts_with("gpa"))))

[1] 1200

# the number of non-missing gpa cells in the wide data equals the number of
# rows in the long data, provided gpa is never missing in the long format


gpa2long |>
  summarise(
    mean_gpa = mean(gpa, na.rm = TRUE),
    n = sum(!is.na(gpa))
  )

# A tibble: 1 × 2
  mean_gpa     n
     <dbl> <int>
1     2.87  1200

gpa2wide |>
  pivot_longer(
    starts_with("gpa"),
    values_to = "gpa"

  summarise(
    mean_gpa = mean(gpa, na.rm = TRUE),

# the same mean and the same number of values: nothing was lost or invented

Save the wide dataset.

write_rds(gpa2wide, "data/gpa2wide.rds")
# .rds stores a single R object, preserving all types and attributes

Load it again and convert back to long format.

gpa2wide_reloaded <- read_rds("data/gpa2wide.rds")

gpa2long_again <- gpa2wide_reloaded |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = -c(student, sex, highgpa, admitted),
    names_to = c(".value", "occas"),
    names_pattern = "(.*)_t(.*)"
  ) |>
  mutate(occas = as.numeric(occas))
# ".value" tells pivot_longer that this part of the name becomes the new
# variable name, while the remainder becomes the value of occas

2. Sex-specific country indicators
Inspect the variable names.

names(world95)

 [1] "country"  "populatn" "density"  "urban"    "religion" "lifeexpf"
 [7] "lifeexpm" "literacy" "pop_incr" "babymort" "gdp_cap"  "region"

# look for the sex-specific pairs


# gender-specific: lifeexpm and lifeexpf, lit_male and lit_female
# not gender-specific: country, populatn, density, and the remaining variables
#
# The two pairs do not follow the same naming convention: one uses a suffix
# without a separator, the other an underscore and a full word. pivot_longer()
# needs a single consistent pattern, so we rename first.

Rename to a consistent convention.

world95_renamed <- world95 |>
  rename(
    lifeexp_male = lifeexpm,
    lifeexp_female = lifeexpf,
    lit_male = lit_male,
    lit_female = lit_fema,
    population = populatn
  )

  select(country, population, density, starts_with("lifeexp"), starts_with("lit")) |>
  slice(1:5)

world95_long <- world95_long |>

ii. Long-long-wide-wide

level4_llww <- level4 |>

    id_cols = c(hhid, iid, urban, male, edu),
    names_from = year,
    values_from = c(att1, att2, att3)

# the time dimension moves into the variable names


names(level4_llww)

[1] 8

# nine attitude variables: three items times three years
# one row per individual


# What does an observation represent?
#
# One person. Households and individuals are still long, so partners occupy
# separate rows linked by hhid, but all measurements of a person, across
# both items and years, are now stored side by side in that person's row.
# This is the format that structural equation modelling usually expects.
#
# Note that edu is listed in id_cols. That is only correct if edu does not
# change over the years within a person. If it did, pivot_wider() would treat
# each value as a separate person and produce too many rows.


level4 |>
  summarise(n_edu = n_distinct(edu), .by = iid) |>
  summarise(max_n_edu = max(n_edu))

# A tibble: 1 × 1
  max_n_edu
